title: Bobcat
wiki_lead:
The bobcat (Lynx rufus), also known as the wildcat, bay lynx, or red lynx, is one of the four extant species within the medium-sized wild cat genus Lynx. Native to North America, it ranges from southern Canada through most of the contiguous United States to Oaxaca in Mexico. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List since 2002, due to its wide distribution and large population. Although it has been hunted extensively both for sport and fur, populations have proven stable, though declining in some areas.
It has distinctive black bars on its forelegs and a black-tipped, stubby (or "bobbed") tail, from which it derives its name. It reaches a total length (including the tail) of up to 125 cm (50 in). It is an adaptable predator inhabiting wooded areas, semidesert, urban edge, forest edge, and swampland environments. It remains in some of its original range, but populations are vulnerable to extirpation by coyotes and domestic animals. 
Though the bobcat prefers rabbits and hares, it hunts insects, chickens, geese and other birds, small rodents, and deer. Prey selection depends on location and habitat, season, and abundance. Like most cats, the bobcat is territorial and largely solitary, although with some overlap in home ranges. It uses several methods to mark its territorial boundaries, including claw marks and deposits of urine or feces. The bobcat breeds from winter into spring and has a gestation period of about two months.
Two subspecies are recognized: one east of the Great Plains, and the other west of the Great Plains. It is featured in some stories of the indigenous peoples of North and Central America, and in the folklore of European-descended inhabitants of the Americas.

Taxonomy and evolution
Felis rufa was the scientific name proposed by Johann Christian Daniel von Schreber in 1777. In the 19th and 20th centuries, the following zoological specimens were described:

Lynx floridanus proposed by Constantine Samuel Rafinesque in 1817 was a greyish lynx with yellowish brown spots from Florida.
Lynx fasciatus also proposed by Rafinesque in 1817 was a reddish-brown lynx with thick fur from the northwest coast.
Lynx baileyi proposed by Clinton Hart Merriam in 1890 was a female lynx that was shot in the San Francisco Mountains.
Lynx texensis proposed by Joel Asaph Allen in 1895 to replace the earlier name Lynx rufus var. maculatus.
Lynx gigas proposed by Outram Bangs in 1897 was a skin of an adult male lynx shot near Bear River, Nova Scotia.
Lynx rufus eremicus and Lynx rufus californicus proposed by Edgar Alexander Mearns in 1898 were skins and skulls of two adult lynxes killed in San Diego County, California.

grok_lead: The bobcat ( Lynx rufus) is a medium-sized wild cat native to North America, renowned for its adaptability and distinctive appearance, including reddish-brown fur mottled with black spots and stripes, prominent tufted ears, facial ruffs, and a short, bobbed tail measuring 4 to 7 inches long that inspires its common name. Adults typically weigh 15 to 35 pounds and measure 26 to 41 inches in body length, with males generally larger than females, making them roughly twice the size of a domestic cat. Bobcats exhibit a broad distribution across much of North America, ranging from southern Canada through the United States to central Mexico, and absent only from Delaware. They thrive in diverse habitats, including forests, semi-deserts, mountains, brushlands, swamps, and even urban edges, preferring areas with dense cover for concealment and hunting. As solitary, territorial animals active primarily at dawn, dusk, and night, bobcats are expert stalkers and ambush predators, relying on keen senses, powerful hind legs for leaps up to 12 feet, and climbing abilities to capture prey. Their diet is opportunistic and carnivorous, consisting mainly of rabbits, rodents, birds, reptiles, and occasionally larger animals like deer fawns, supplemented by scavenging or insects. Despite historical hunting pressures for fur and pelts, bobcat populations have rebounded due to their resilience and conservation efforts, with an estimated 2 to 3 million individuals across their range. The species is classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, reflecting its wide distribution, stable numbers, and lack of major threats, though habitat fragmentation and vehicle collisions pose localized risks. Bobcats play a vital ecological role as mesopredators, helping regulate rodent and small mammal populations in their ecosystems.
